title: Mikaela Shiffrin Returns to Killington for World Cup GS - Ski Racing Media
content: Mikaela Shiffrin returns to Killington, Vermont, on Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026, for her first Superstar race since her 2024 crash. Shiffrin (🇺🇸 USA), a Stifel Alpine Ambassador, will chase her first giant slalom win at the Stifel Killington Cup on Saturday and make her season slalom debut on Sunday. Shiffrin led the opening run in Sölden, Austria, on Oct. 24 and finished seventh. Her Stifel U.S. Ski Team teammate 🇺🇸 USA Paula Moltzan won by a hundredth of a second for her first World Cup victory. Saturday’s Stifel Killington Cup brings both racers to a hill where no U.S. woman has won a World Cup GS. On Nov. 30, 2024, Shiffrin took a 0.32-second lead into the second run. She was chasing her 100th World Cup win and her first GS victory at Killington. She crashed late in the run and suffered a deep puncture wound that injured her abdominal muscles. FIS race report “That was the best skiing I’ve ever done in Killington,” Shiffrin told Pat Graham of The Associated Press. She said she has worked with her sports psychologist ahead of the return. Acknowledging what scares her, she told the AP, helps her focus on the gates once she starts. Shiffrin spoke publicly about post-traumatic stress after the crash and sat out the giant slalom at the 2025 world championships in Saalbach, Austria. She raced slalom in the team combined there and won gold with 🇺🇸 USA Breezy Johnson. Later that month, she earned World Cup win No. 100 in slalom at Sestriere, Italy. SRM’s reporting from Saalbach · FIS team combined report · FIS report on win No. 100 Shiffrin trained at Vermont’s Burke Mountain Academy before joining the World Cup circuit. On Superstar, she has reached three GS podiums, including a second-place finish in 2017. She holds the women’s World Cup record with 22 GS wins, but her last came in December 2023 in Lienz, Austria. She has made 18 World Cup GS starts since then. The Stifel Alpine Ambassador has put more of her training and race schedule behind GS and super-G this winter. Shiffrin announced the shift in October on her podcast, “What’s the Point,” and said she would race a lighter slalom schedule. She skipped Levi and Gurgl, making Sunday, Nov. 29, her first slalom start since a season in which she won nine of 10 World Cup slaloms and Olympic gold in the discipline. title: Heungkuk Life Falls to Fifth Loss in Post-Kim Era - 조선일보
content: Silva's 30-point performance leads GS Caltex; Heungkuk Life five points from last [OSEN=Lee Hoo-kwang Reporter] Heungkuk Life, navigating the post-Kim Yeon-koung era, has faced a critical crisis. Heungkuk Life, led by coach Yoshihara Tomoko, suffered a complete defeat with a set score of 0-3 (19-25, 22-25, 29-31) in their home game against GS Caltex in the second round of the HK Heungkuk Financial 2026-2027 V-League women’s division, held at Incheon Samsan World Gymnasium on November 27. Heungkuk Life fell into a five-game losing streak, remaining in sixth place with 2 wins, 5 losses (6 points). The point gap with the last-placed SOOP remains at 5 points. Meanwhile, GS Caltex, on a five-game winning streak, overtook Korea Expressway Corporation and rose to first place. They tied with Korea Expressway Corporation at 6 wins and 1 draw (18 points) but claimed the top spot due to a superior set ratio. The absence of a reliable ace like Kim Yeon-koung was evident in the match. Pyo Seung-joo scored 13 points (40% attack success rate), Kindelan 12 points (35.48%), and Justice 11 points (36.36%). However, 16 unforced errors (5 more than the opponent) also contributed to the loss. After a service error by the opponent brought the third set to 23-24, a net touch error occurred at 29-29, and Kindelan’s attack was blocked by Tanacha, finalizing the five-game losing streak. GS Caltex’s foreign player Silva dominated with 30 points and a 62.50% attack success rate. She added 11 back-row attacks, 3 blocks, and 2 service aces, narrowly missing a triple crown by one service ace. Choi Ga-eun contributed 12 points (90.91% attack success rate), and Tanacha added 10 points (40%). Heungkuk Life will challenge to break their losing streak on December 1 in a home game against Hyundai Engineering & Construction. GS Caltex aims for a sixth consecutive win on December 3 in a home game against the Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK). In the men’s division match held at the same time at Gyeyang Gymnasium in Incheon, Korean Air narrowly defeated KB Insurance with a set score of 3-1 (25-19, 32-34, 26-24, 26-24), extending their winning streak to three games. Getzinsky scored 25 points, and Lim Dong-hyok contributed 20 points.

title: The Forgotten Lexus V8 That Made German Rivals Work Harder - Top Speed
content: Somewhere between the turbo boom and the electric rush, a Japanese sedan showed up with an engine its German rivals had already abandoned. It revved to 7,300 rpm, breathed without forced induction, and sounded like a race car idling outside a boardroom. It never sold in mass numbers, never swept a comparison test with top honors, and its maker never marketed it with much swagger. Yet drivers kept asking the same mildly irritated question. Why did nobody make more noise about this? Now that the performance sedan class has changed so completely, that question has become a lot more interesting. By the time the Lexus GS F arrived for the 2016 model year, the German establishment had already made its choice. BMW's 5.0-liter V10 left the M5 after 2010, replaced by a twin-turbocharged 4.4-liter V8. Mercedes-AMG retired its wailing 6.3-liter V8 from the E63 and swapped in a 5.5-liter biturbo. On paper, both moves were obvious. Turbos delivered more torque, better fuel economy numbers, and quicker acceleration. What they took away was the direct connection between your right foot and the engine. Forced induction smooths out the delivery, flattens the soundtrack, and moves the thrill from the top of the rev range to the middle. The Germans traded some theater for on-paper numbers. Lexus went the other way. It kept a naturally aspirated V8 and built the sedan around it. That wasn't nostalgia for its own sake. It was a company that had never played the Nürburgring lap-time game deciding to offer something different. The result felt like a deliberate throwback the moment you pressed the start button. The 2UR-GSE is a 5.0-liter V8 developed with Yamaha, making 467 horsepower at 7,100 rpm and 389 pound-feet of torque between 4,800 and 5,600 rpm. The redline sits at 7,300 rpm, which is serious territory for a V8 of this size. Titanium intake valves help it spin freely, and the engine can switch to Atkinson-cycle operation at light loads to save fuel. Even so, the headline trait is how hungrily it climbs through the revs. Power goes to the rear wheels through an eight-speed automatic with a Torsen limited-slip differential. Lexus claimed a 0-to-60-mph time of about 4.5 seconds and a top speed of 168 mph. Those are strong numbers, though not class-leading. The soundtrack deserves its own special mention. Lexus piped induction noise into the cabin and tuned the exhaust for a hard-edged bark on the way up the rev range. Take a run down the Pacific Coast Highway, for instance, with the windows down. Here the V8 pulls cleanly through the gears, the engine note sharpens past 5,000 rpm, and the canyon wall throws it back at you. It feels engaging rather than merely quick, and that's a distinction spec sheets rarely capture when it comes to a naturally aspirated V8. The F10-generation BMW M5 made a stout 560 horsepower and 502 pound-feet, rising to 575 horsepower with the Competition Package. The E63 AMG S 4MATIC produced a mammoth 577 horsepower and 590 pound-feet. Both ran zero to 60 mph in under four seconds, comfortably ahead of the Lexus, and the all-wheel-drive Mercedes could put its power down far more easily in the wet. When the next-generation M5 and E63 arrived around 2018, the gap grew wider still. On outright pace and technology, the Germans win with their turbocharged grunt. The Lexus GS F's case rests elsewhere when compared to its period rivals. First, there's the throttle response. With no turbos to spool, the V8 reacts the instant you ask. Second, the rev ceiling. An engine that happily spins to 7,300 rpm rewards being driven hard in a way a torque-rich turbo motor rarely does. Third, there is the ownership confidence. The Lexus has no turbochargers, no charge-air plumbing, and none of the heat management that comes with them, which should mean fewer expensive surprises as the miles pile up. The value argument shows up on the used market too. A clean GS F generally costs far less than a comparable M5 or E63 of the same era, and its running costs should be lower too. That isn't a claim of outright superiority; however, it's a claim about what you get per dollar and the peace of mind that comes with the Lexus reputation for reliability. Lexus built its reputation on cars that simply keep working, and the GS F inherits that. The cabin is solidly assembled, the seats are supportive without being punishing, and the ride, while firm, stays livable on broken pavement. A freeway commute is perfectly civilized, with the V8 settling into a hushed murmur at 70 mph. It isn't a flawless package though. The infotainment system and its touchpad-style controller have aged poorly. The automatic gearbox is smooth but lacks the sharp reflexes of a dual-clutch unit. At roughly 4,000 pounds, the car carries real weight, and fuel economy drops fast when you use the top of the rev range. The EPA rates it at 16 mpg city, 24 mpg highway, and 19 mpg combined. Still, the pitch is clear. You get a genuine performance car with a long-term reliability reputation, plus the mechanical simplicity that makes an older example feel less risky than a similarly aged turbocharged rival. For many buyers, that blend is rarer than raw horsepower. Production was small compared with the M5 and E63, and the GS F left the US market after the 2020 model year. That's the foundation of any collectibility argument. Naturally aspirated V8 sedans are close to extinct, and the market is starting to notice. Examples with full service histories and unmodified specs are the ones to chase. Several things count in its favor as a used purchase: the engine is shared with other Lexus performance models, including the LC 500, which supports long-term parts availability. The ownership experience is also less likely to involve costly turbo-related repairs, and depreciation has largely run its course, so values look steadier than those of comparable German rivals. When shopping, look for service records from an authorized Lexus dealer, tire condition (the car is hard on rear rubber), brake wear, and any signs of track abuse. Insurance and fuel costs will still sting, so budget accordingly. The GS F is not the fastest car in its class, and it never pretended to be. It's a charismatic, durable, and increasingly scarce alternative, and the Germans, who spent years making their V8s cleverer rather than more characterful, never quite answered it. Buy one now, and you're getting the last of a kind at a price that probably won't last. We want to hear from you. GS Caltex secured a victory away from home against Heungkuk Life, led by the performance of their "top scorer" Silva. In the second round of the women's division of the "HK Heungkuk Financial 2026~2027 V-League" held at Samseong World Gymnasium in Bupyeong-gu, Incheon, at 7 p.m. on the 27th, GS Caltex defeated Heungkuk Life away from home with a set score of 3-0 (25-19, 25-22, 31-29). title: GS E&C Turns Model Homes Into Art-Filled Experience Galleries - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Mokdong Yunseul Xi Features Ned Kahn Installation, Media Screening Room
Suji Xi Edicion Model Home Lets Visitors Try Community Services GS E&C (006360.KS) is reshaping its Xi model homes into spaces where visitors can view artwork and preview life after move-in. The builder plans to add exhibitions and community service demonstrations to its sales consultations and floor-plan tours to showcase the residential character of each complex. GS E&C said on Nov. 27 that it is expanding its "experiential housing gallery" concept across Xi model homes. The company is extending the gallery-style format first introduced at House Xi, which opened in Daechi-dong, Gangnam District, Seoul, in 2024 to coincide with a revamp of the Xi brand, to individual presale complexes. At the Armusee Xi model home, the layout guides visitors through a complex model and media exhibition before they tour community facilities and unit interiors and receive sales consultations. GS E&C has created a product strategy committee involving its marketing, sales and design teams to factor a complex's location, surrounding infrastructure and customer profile into model home planning. The Mokdong Yunseul Xi model home features a work created in collaboration with environmental artist Ned Kahn that captures the movement of light and wind. Alongside a media screening room, the model home also recreates a guest house, one of the complex's community facilities for residents. The Suji Xi Edicion model home in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, recreates a cafe and shower facilities and allows visitors to sample Book Curation, a book recommendation service from Kyobo Book Centre, and Gourmet, a food and beverage service. The Doryong Xi Lafique model home recreates the outdoor Jacuzzi that is one of the complex's signature amenities. "Model homes are a key point of contact where customers directly experience the Xi brand," a GS E&C official said. "We will continue to deliver inspiration and value beyond simply residential space through experiential housing galleries that combine design, art and differentiated lifestyle content." content: BMW Motorrad launched the F 900 GS Sport in Brazil, a new version of its middleweight adventure motorcycle, at a promotional price of R$79,990. The announcement was made on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Specifications are available in the BMW Brazil press release, published in São Paulo. Motonline and Motociclismo Online covered the motorcycle in detail on Tuesday, November 24, and also list its price, engine and equipment. GWM confirms R$149,990 ORA 5 BEV45 for Brazil, with a 45.3-kWh battery and 177 hp; new electric version arrives in January Brazil’s tire industry sells more than 3 million fewer tires in 2026 as volume falls 10.4% to its lowest level since 2019 Manufacturer invests R$25 million in Guarulhos, modernizes plant and adopts anticorrosion coating for hoods on the Onix, HB20, Strada and Polo Ford confirms Bronco Basecamp with more than 400 hp and up to 1,200 km of range for Brazil in 2027 The video above is from the MOTOO channel and was posted on August 5, 2024. It takes a detailed look at the 2025 F 900 GS, the model on which the Sport version is based. For Brazilian riders, the new model comes standard with Pro Riding Modes and Shift Assistant Pro. BMW Motorrad says the version makes the GS lineup more accessible in Brazil. The R$79,990 price is a promotional launch price, according to BMW Motorrad. The same offer is listed by Motonline, Motociclismo Online, Vrum and MOTOO. The F 900 GS Sport is available in Brazil in a single color: blue. The press release places the version in the Adventure segment and says its configuration strengthens the model’s competitiveness. The motorcycle comes with a three-year warranty. The term is stated in BMW Brazil’s official release and is also listed by Vrum, MOTOO and Motociclismo Online. The manufacturer says the Sport’s arrival is part of a strategy to maintain a diverse lineup. Its stated goal is to serve different types of riders and attract new customers. The engine is an 895cc liquid-cooled inline twin with eight valves. It produces 90 hp at 6,750 rpm, according to BMW Motorrad. MOTOO, Vrum and Motociclismo Online report the same 90 hp at the same engine speed. Motonline lists both power and torque at 6,750 rpm. Outside Brazil, the F 900 GS has a different engine tune. A global BMW press release dated September 7, 2023, lists 77 kW, or 105 hp, at 8,500 rpm. The same figure appears in a test published by U.S. magazine Cycle News on July 19, 2024: 105 hp at 8,500 rpm. BMW Motorrad presents the Sport version’s package as a combination of performance, efficiency and versatility. It is designed for both long highway trips and off-road stretches. BMW Motorrad’s U.S. account posted an image of the middleweight GS lineup on X on January 29, 2024. The post says the three  motorcycles are ready for their next adventure: the F 900 GS, F 900 GS Adventure and F 800 GS. It then asks readers which one is their favorite. United by the #SpiritOfGS, the #F900GS, #F900GSAdventure and #F800GS are eager for their next adventure! Which one is your favorite?#HungryForMore #BMWMotorrad #MakeLifeARide pic.twitter.com/9dexMp8awy — bmwmotorradusa (@BMWMotorradUSA) January 29, 2024 The official torque figure is 93 Nm at 6,750 rpm, the same  engine speed at which maximum power is reached. The figure appears in BMW Brazil’s announcement and the company’s 2023 global announcement. Brazilian websites converted the torque figure to kilogram-force meters, with differing results. Motonline reported 9.3 kgf·m, MOTOO listed 9.4 kgf·m, Motociclismo Online used 9.48 kgf·m, and Vrum gave 9 kgf·m. Car Blog and the Motor Mais website use the manufacturer’s 93 Nm figure. BMW Motorrad’s figure is the reference value. In the United States, Cycle News lists torque in pound-feet: 68.6 lb-ft at 6,750 rpm. That is the same engine speed listed in the Brazilian specifications. The transmission has six speeds. Shift Assistant Pro, BMW Motorrad’s shift assistant, comes standard on the F 900 GS Sport. The system allows riders to shift up and down without using the clutch, depending on operating conditions, Motociclismo Online explains. Motonline describes the same clutch-free use of the transmission. Motonline says Pro Riding Modes and the shift assistant are the features the Sport adds to the F 900 GS. The site describes them as more performance-oriented. Pro Riding Modes are standard equipment. In its 2023 global announcement, BMW says the F 900 GS has Rain and Road modes, ABS Pro and DTC traction control. The same announcement says the Pro package adds extra modes and mode preselection. It also includes engine drag torque control and Dynamic Brake Control, or DBC. The bike has a TFT display with connectivity through BMW Motorrad Connected, which links the motorcycle to a phone. The screen measures 6.5 inches, according to BMW’s global announcement and Vrum, which reviewed the Pro version in July. On the Duas Rodas magazine channel, journalist and rider Leandro Mello tests the F 900 GS in a video dated April 17, 2026. He evaluates the engine, riding modes, suspension and ergonomics. The Akrapovič muffler comes standard on the F 900 GS Sport. It is listed in BMW Motorrad’s announcement, MOTOO, Vrum and Motociclismo Online. Heated grips and hand guards are standard equipment. The lighting is full LED. The bike has keyless ignition through the Keyless system, which Motonline calls a proximity key. In its 2023 global announcement, BMW lists Keyless Ride as a factory option on the F 900 GS. Motonline says the standard F 900 GS already comes in Brazil with a proximity key, suspension adjustment, heated grips and an Akrapovič muffler. In the official Sport equipment list, the Akrapovič muffler appears alongside Pro Riding Modes and Shift Assistant Pro, all listed as standard equipment. The Sport’s suspension offers preload, compression and rebound adjustment. The brake and shift levers are adjustable. Both features are mentioned in BMW Motorrad’s announcement and in articles by Motociclismo Online, Vrum and MOTOO. On the F 900 GS Pro, BMW uses the Enduro Pro package. It includes a fully adjustable Showa front fork, a ZF/Sachs rear shock, a black handlebar with a riser and an M Endurance chain. Blue is the only color available in Brazil. Motonline calls the shade Snapper Rocks Blue and describes some of the bodywork in that color, a black base and a white rear frame. BMW Motorrad’s press photos show the F 900 GS Sport with a blue fuel tank and side panels, a black seat, a light-colored subframe and an Akrapovič muffler on the right side. In Brazil, the Sport is priced below the F 900 GS Pro São Paulo Yellow. BMW Motorrad launched the Pro on July 20, 2026, at R$93,990. Vrum reported the same price for the Pro on July 21, 2026. Both versions use an 895-cc  engine rated at 90 hp and 93 Nm in the Brazilian specifications. The Pro adds the Enduro Pro package and a tall windscreen. The F 900 GS Sport is available for a promotional price of R$79,990 and comes standard with the Pro Riding Modes electronics, Shift Assistant Pro and a three-year warranty. BMW Motorrad’s global account on X highlighted its F 900 GS Adventure sibling on March 12, 2024. The post, written in English, says the  motorcycle offers full touring capability in Thailand or the Black Forest, on mountain roads or highways. Whether in Thailand or the Black Forest, high mountain passes or highways, the F 900 GS Adventure delivers perfect touring capability. title: Tommy G’s Clubhouse to serve Pensacola adults 22+ with disabilities at no cost - WEAR-TV
content: PENSACOLA, Fla. -- For many families who have loved ones with special needs, finding a place where they can socialize is often a challenge. A new space in Pensacola aims to change that. It's called Tommy G's Clubhouse, and it's being built specifically for adults 22 and older with intellectual disabilities. From arts and crafts, video games, a sensory room, a computer lab, and a library, Tommy G's Clubhouse will serve as a space where people with disabilities and their caretakers can connect free of charge. "Not everybody can work; not everybody has the capability to go in and do a four- or five- or eight-hour-a-day job, but they still need something to do," co-owner of Tommy G's Clubhouse Keith Grayam said. "They need a place to belong. We don't want them sitting at home and watching TV or playing a game system or just wishing they could be somewhere. So that's what's important about here." "He is 40 years old and operates at about a seven-year-old level. For a long time, I was a single father," Grayam said. "Wishing that I had some place to take my son other than just out for a drive or walking at the mall." That's how the concept of a special needs social and learning space was formed. "We are actually taking this room and turning it into a studio apartment," Grayam said. "We're going to help teach life skills in here. We'll have a bed in here, a stove, and a refrigerator." "Our friends can come in and work on making the bed and folding clothes and learning how to do the day-to-day chores that they're expected to do at home, too," he added. Co-owner Helen Rasberry says adults with special needs often age out of school programs by 22 and suddenly find themselves with fewer opportunities to connect with others. "We've just learned in the last year and a half that there are just not enough services out there for those with special needs," Rasberry said. "They can't necessarily participate in all of the things that everyone else participates in, and there are holes in the system, and people fall through." Before purchasing the building, clients enrolled in Tommy G's used to go on social outings together -- bowling, shopping, and interacting. "When we decided we needed a building, we thought we would find something small and just have a place for ourselves," Grayam said. "Then Helen was driving down the road and saw this building and called me, and we came in and went, 'Okay, we're not ready for this, but let's take a leap of faith and jump.' And that's what we did." The clubhouse will also have an enclosed outdoor yard with a sensory swing and outdoor pizza kitchen.

title: GS Caltex Employees Pack 200 Winter Kits for Yeosu Residents - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
"Sharing Warmth" Volunteer Drive Heats Up Community Outreach
Employees Assemble 200 Winter Kits by Hand YEOSU — Employees of GS Caltex have gathered to help vulnerable residents in Yeosu who face both the winter cold and the burden of heating bills. The company said on the 26th that it held a "Sharing Warmth" volunteer event on the 25th at the conference room of the Yeosu City Community Social Security Council. About 30 employee volunteers took part and assembled 200 winter kits by hand. The volunteers checked and packed seven types of cold-weather items needed in winter, including thermal cushions, neck warmers, knit gloves, beanies, heat packs, KF94 masks and earmuffs. The kits contained more than just winter supplies. They also carried the employees' wish that their neighbors facing the cold months ahead would stay a little warmer. The completed kits will be delivered to older adults in vulnerable households and to families with members who have disabilities through the Yeosu City Senior Welfare Center, the Yeosu City Welfare Center for the Disabled and the Yeosu City Community Social Security Council. "It is a small gesture, but we hope it brings warm comfort to our neighbors in the community," a GS Caltex official said. "We will continue to look closely after those in need and carry on sharing with the local community." GS Caltex runs a range of community programs, including support for families in crisis through its "1,000-Won Happiness" small-donation campaign, the "Chuseok Sharing Warmth" drive and "Saerom Class," a program supporting the development of young people. title: FIRST RIDE | BMW F450 GS makes adventure riding more accessible - TimesLIVE
content: BMW Motorrad has launched the new F450 GS as its entry-level adventure motorcycle in South Africa. Replacing the single-cylinder G310 GS, it is a more powerful machine with a twin-cylinder 420cc engine and is BMW’s latest contender in the growing market segment of medium-displacement bikes. Like its larger stablemates in the GS range, it is a versatile all-rounder, combining everyday usability, touring comfort and off-road capability. Its more accessible price and manageable power output should appeal to beginners without disappointing more experienced riders. The bike’s tractable power delivery is one of the things that impressed me most when I rode it at the South African media launch in Gauteng earlier this week. On roads that took us along popular breakfast-run routes in Hartbeespoort, as well as on gravel trails, the engine felt punchier than I expected for its small size. The parallel-twin engine, with outputs of 35kW at 8,750 rpm and 43Nm at 6,750 rpm, proved to have a free-revving nature that gave the medium-sized bike a zesty spring in its step, whether pulling off or overtaking slower traffic. With a top speed of around 170km/h, it has good touring potential too, and the small screen provides decent wind protection at higher speeds. With claimed fuel consumption of 3.8l/100km, the bike has a range of more than 350km on its 14l tank. The engine has a single balance shaft to reduce vibrations and it’s mostly effective, though I felt some buzzy vibrations through the seat at certain revs. The unit has a characteristically fruity twin-cylinder sound without being too noisy. It is packed with much of the technology found in its more expensive stablemates, including standard traction control, engine drag control, heated grips and lean-angle-sensitive anti-lock braking All versions of the bike except the basic version have a quickshifter, which allows clutchless up- and downshifts in the six-speed transmission. Standard on the GS Trophy and optionally available on the other variants is an Easy Ride Clutch (ERC). Using a centrifugal clutch, it allows you to operate the bike without the clutch lever, even when pulling off, but allows the rider to intervene manually at any time if necessary. The F450 GS is a mid-sized bike that won’t feel too intimidating to novice riders. Weighing 178kg, it is a lot smaller and wieldier than the big daddy R1300 GS, which tips the scales at a portly 238kg, but retains the typical GS sense of heft and solid feel, with high-quality finishes. Available in three saddle heights to accommodate various-sized riders, the 450 is also unmistakably a GS in design, with its distinctive flyline, tough-guy looks, tubular steel frame and features such as an LED headlight with an “X” daytime riding light. It is also packed with much of the technology found in its more expensive stablemates, including standard traction control, engine drag control, heated grips and lean-angle-sensitive anti-lock braking. All models have three riding modes — Rain, Road and Enduro — with an additional Enduro Pro mode from the Exclusive model upwards. The latter disables the ABS assistance on the rear wheel, allowing the rider to lock the wheel deliberately when necessary on gravel, giving greater control over braking. On off-road sections of the route, the F450 GS excelled with its comfortable ride and reassuring agility. I was particularly impressed with how yielding the suspension was and how effectively it absorbed bumpy, rippled surfaces. There was no chance to test it in soft sand, but on rough gravel the middleweight BMW displayed the classic GS turf-taming ability. Wider enduro footrests are included from the Exclusive version upwards or are available as optional accessories. The front wheel is guided via KYB upside-down telescopic forks, while the rear wheel has a double-arm swingarm with a KYB central spring strut featuring progressive damping. The Sport and GS Trophy variants feature sports suspension that allows the rider to adjust both rebound and compression damping. All but the base model have handguards and wide off-road footrests, while the range-topping GS Trophy has an aluminium engine guard. The brakes comprise a single 310mm front disc with a Brembo four-piston fixed caliper and a single 240mm rear disc. The F450 GS comes standard with aluminium alloy wheels (19-inch front and 17-inch rear), but is optionally available with more trail-focused spoked wheels. The dual-purpose Maxxis tubeless tyres provided good grip both on and off the tar. The 6.5-inch TFT display is legible in sunlight and menus are accessed via an iDrive-style rotary controller. There is a USB-C socket, and taking phone calls, listening to music and using navigation while riding are all possible via smartphone and helmet pairing. title: Vikran Engineering faces ₹12.50 crore claim in litigation with GS Products India - Business Upturn
content: Vikran Engineering Limited has disclosed a significant legal development concerning a claim raised by M/s. GS Products India amounting to ₹12.50 crore. The company made this announcement in compliance with Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, following an administrative warning from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) dated 4th November 2026. The litigation involves a claim that was presented by GS Products India to the MSME Facilitation Council in October 2025. As of now, Vikran Engineering has responded to the claim, but no further communication regarding subsequent proceedings has been received by the company. This latest disclosure from Vikran Engineering was necessitated by SEBI's advice aiming for enhanced governance, transparency, and investor awareness. The company's board of directors discussed the matter in their meeting on 5th November 2026, where they acknowledged SEBI's communication and pledged to ensure continued transparency in their operations. Despite the substantial claim, Vikran Engineering Limited's current assessment indicates an anticipated additional financial liability of approximately ₹1.81 crore if an adverse order is passed by the competent authority. This estimate was initially assessed as falling below the materiality threshold of ₹3.26 crore as of 31st March 2025, thus impacting the immediacy and nature of prior disclosures. The company emphasised that this disclosure is part of its continued commitment to transparency, ensuring stakeholders are informed about the current situation and its potential financial implications. More details of the litigation, including particulars of the dispute, expected financial implications, and quantum of claims, were attached in an annexure to the formal announcement. The ongoing matter remains a point of concern for Vikran Engineering Limited as they await any further action or communication from the MSME Facilitation Council. The company continues to monitor the situation closely, reiterating its commitment to keeping all relevant parties informed as more information becomes available. title: NBA Power Rankings: Whom is each team most thankful for this year? - ESPN
content:
As the NBA plays its final games Wednesday night before the Thanksgiving holiday, there is plenty to celebrate around the association as the first full month of the season winds down. MVP front-runners Luka Doncic and Victor Wembanyama have jumped out to sizzling starts, adding to their already impressive résumés as they lead the Los Angeles Lakers and San Antonio Spurs to the top two spots in the West. Meanwhile, Doncic's former Lakers teammate LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers have surged to the top of the East. The Miami Heat are certainly grateful to be the winners of the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes, riding a seven-game win streak after dropping their first four games of the season. And the Portland Trail Blazers have welcomed Damian Lillard back with open arms, coming off a blowout win over James and the Sixers on Monday night. In this week's Power Rankings, our insiders rank each of the 30 teams and also highlight one player, coach or executive each team should be thankful for as we celebrate Thanksgiving -- with some lamb chops and gravy, of course. Previous rankings: Preseason | Oct. 28 | Nov. 4 | Nov. 11 | Nov. 18 Jump to a team:
ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE
DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND
LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN
NO | NY | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX
POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS Next games: @ POR (Nov. 25), vs. LAL (Nov. 27), vs. BOS (Nov. 29), @ MIL (Nov. 30) In switching to the current guard-heavy starting lineup, San Antonio needed to find ways to optimize the group around franchise superstar Victor Wembanyama. What better way to do that than by bringing in a veteran assistant in Hall of Famer Donovan, who has extensive expertise in that area? Throughout his head coaching tenure in Oklahoma City, Donovan worked with a bevy of dynamic guards such as Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Russell Westbrook, Chris Paul and Dennis Schroder, and understands how to make the spacing work with so many perimeter players on the court together at the same time. The Spurs' new lineup isn't a finished product yet, but the addition of Donovan is helping it round into form quickly. -- Michael C. Wright Next games: @ SA (Nov. 27), @ MEM (Nov. 29), @ HOU (Nov. 30) The 27-year-old supernova is on the short list for the way-too-early MVP contenders (shoutout to our former colleague and current Atlanta Hawks front office member, Tim Bontemps) and has been electric to watch this season, averaging a career-best 36.6 points. It's not only Doncic's scoring that has been a boon for L.A. as it has stayed atop the Western Conference standings. Doncic's sturdy defense -- more recently as a roamer in the Lakers' full-court zone defense and throughout the season with his one-on-one containment (he is second in the NBA in charges drawn) -- caused one team source to tell ESPN that Doncic has been playing "the best defense of his life." -- Dave McMenamin Next games: vs. MIA (Nov. 25), @ IND (Nov. 27), @ HOU (Nov. 28), vs. MEM (Dec. 1) The Sixers play in front of one of the NBA's most passionate fanbases, but also one of its most scorned. It has been 43 years since the Sixers' last title, and for the past decade they endured the infamous tanking era, massive injuries and years of heartbreaking second-round exits. James' signing gave this fanbase real championship hope after years of disappointment. And his impact has been felt early, as the Sixers are off to their best start since 2000-01, which happens to be their most recent finals appearance. -- Kris Rhim Next games: @ OKC (Nov. 25), vs. MEM (Nov. 27), @ SAC (Nov. 29), @ POR (Dec. 1) The Timberwolves didn't officially sign Kuminga until September, months after most of this summer's free agents found new homes. But the long wait has been worth it for both sides: With Minnesota buying time for Anthony Edwards to return from knee surgery, Kuminga has provided valuable contributions on both ends. The athletic forward has averaged 13.4 points and shot 39.7% on 3-pointers in a complementary offensive role, and he's part of a well-balanced starting lineup that has posted an excellent plus-10 net rating without Edwards. -- Ben Golliver Next games: vs. PHX (Nov. 25), vs. PHI (Nov. 28), vs. LAL (Nov. 30), vs. TOR (Dec. 1) Perhaps it's too early to attribute Amen Thompson's shooting improvements to Houston's decision to bring in shooting guru Engelland as an assistant, but you can't discount his track record and reputation around the league, where he's widely regarded as the NBA's best shooting coach. Engelland has worked in the past with Grant Hill, Tony Parker and Kawhi Leonard, along with all of Oklahoma City's young core players, and the results speak for themselves. Thompson should become the latest beneficiary of Engelland's tutelage, along with Reed Sheppard, Jabari Smith Jr. and Tari Eason. -- Wright Next games: vs. CLE (Nov. 25), vs. MIA (Nov. 27), vs. ATL (Nov. 29), @ CHI (Dec. 1) The Knicks look like themselves again, and one big reason has been Towns' consistency. He has had a double-double in every game and leads the NBA in rebounding (13.9). He's playing through the uncertainty of his future as the contract situation hangs over him and the franchise all season long. Still, his shooting splits are ridiculous: 21.8 points on 54/42/76. If there's a reason the Knicks can be counted on to repeat, he's atop the list. -- Vincent Goodwill Next games: @ PHI (Nov. 25), @ NYK (Nov. 27), @ CLE (Nov. 29), vs. ATL (Dec. 1) Despite Giannis Antetokounmpo's MVP-caliber start to the season, we would be remiss to not mention Riley as the person Heat fans should be most thankful for. The list of players Riley has drafted, traded for or signed in Miami is a who's who of current and future Hall of Famers: Alonzo Mourning, Dwyane Wade, Shaquille O'Neal, LeBron James, Chris Bosh, Bam Adebayo, Jimmy Butler and now Antetokounmpo. Miami has won three NBA championships and reached the playoffs in 24 of Riley's 31 seasons with the franchise as head coach and later head of basketball operations. The Antetokounmpo trade has breathed life into a franchise that has not advanced past the first round since the 2022-23 season. -- Bobby Marks Next games: vs. ATL (Nov. 27), @ SA (Nov. 29), @ DAL (Nov. 30) The decision to trade Jaylen Brown for George was so criticized by pundits and Celtics fans alike that even Celtics general manager Brad Stevens acknowledged that fans had a right to be upset about the move. But George has fared well, averaging 19.9 points, 3.8 assists and 5.6 rebounds -- all increases from last season and helping to fuel Boston's top-10 offense. One of his best performances of the season came against his former team, when he scored 36 points in a blowout win earlier this month. -- Rhim Next games: @ UTAH (Nov. 27), @ TOR (Nov. 29), @ DET (Nov. 30) Through 15 games, Murray has been the league's most accurate volume 3-point shooter, making 50 of his 106 attempts. This scorching and efficient scoring from Murray -- 26.2 points on 16.9 shots per game -- has helped the Nuggets sustain a reasonable record (10-5, No. 6 in the West), while many of his teammates are shaking off injury rust and settling into the season. Murray has also received well-deserved plaudits for his improved defensive effort. He is averaging one block and put up this stat line in an overtime win over the Bulls this past weekend: 45 points, seven assists, five rebounds, two blocks, three steals. The Nuggets are plus-96 when he's on the court this season and minus-69 when he's not. -- Anthony Slater Next games: vs. LAC (Nov. 25), @ MIN (Nov. 27), vs. LAL (Nov. 29), @ PHI (Dec. 1) The Memphis general manager slowly dismantled the core of Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane, while embracing a totally new and unconventional style of play to build a different identity with coach Tuomas Isalo. That personnel and philosophical shift took imagination, courage and patience to instill. Grizzlies fans are finally starting to reap the rewards of Kleiman's vision. Memphis signed Ty Jerome in the summer of 2025, and he's averaging a career-high 25.1 points, and selected Cameron Boozer with the third pick of the most recent draft to add to a young core that includes Zach Edey, Cedric Coward and Jaylen Wells. -- Wright Next games: @ BOS (Nov. 27), @ NYK (Nov. 29), @ MIA (Dec. 1) Whom they're thankful for: Nickeil Alexander-Walker Last season's most improved player, Alexander-Walker continues to be one of the best free agents in Hawks history. After averaging a career-high 20.8 PPG last season, Alexander-Walker is averaging 21.3 in two less minutes per game. His $14.4 million salary this season represents one of the better value deals in the league. -- Marks Next games: vs. MIL (Nov. 27), vs. ORL (Nov. 29), vs. DEN (Nov. 30) The Pistons already had Cade Cunningham as their franchise player, along with foundational partners in Jalen Duren and Ausar Thompson, but they endured a record 28-game losing streak in 2023-24. Hiring Bickerstaff to replace Monty Williams one year after Williams had signed a then-record six-year, $78.5 million contract didn't seem as if it would be as fortune-turning as it has been. Bickerstaff has gone 114-66 in two seasons in Detroit, making fans forget how miserable it was before his arrival. The expectations for a deep run into May starts with Bickerstaff's stability on the sidelines, accountability on the court and standards that resonate with the heritage of this franchise -- even staying afloat with the injuries they've suffered this season. -- Goodwill Next games: vs. SA (Nov. 25), vs. GS (Nov. 27), vs. NO (Nov. 29), vs. MIN (Dec. 1) Portland received the ultimate gift when Milwaukee decided to waive and stretch Lillard's contract after his 2025 Achilles tear. Not only did the Blazers get the opportunity to re-sign a franchise icon, but they also snagged Lillard on a bargain contract that pays him $13.4 million in 2026-27 while he remains on Milwaukee's books for $22.5 million every season through 2029-30. Portland is getting All-Star-caliber production from Lillard for its money; Milwaukee is getting absolutely nothing. -- Golliver Next games: vs. MIN (Nov. 25), @ MIL (Nov. 28), @ BKN (Nov. 30) Oklahoma City isn't a franchise that frequently takes big swings in free agency, but general manager Sam Presti strategically targeted Hartenstein in the summer of 2024. Hartenstein proved to be one of the finishing pieces of the Thunder's championship puzzle, providing a physical presence and savvy that Oklahoma City had been missing at center. The veteran, who has averaged a double-double during his Thunder tenure, took a pay cut last summer in signing a three-year, $75 million deal to stay in Oklahoma City. -- Tim MacMahon Fortune favored the Mavs when they won the Flagg sweepstakes, landing the No. 1 pick in the 2025 draft despite only 1.8% odds. Flagg has more than lived up to the hype so far in his NBA career. LeBron James is the only player to record more points, assists and steals than Flagg as a teenager. Months after trading Luka Doncic, Dallas lucked into getting another generational talent to build around. -- MacMahon Next games: @ NYK (Nov. 25), vs. MIA (Nov. 29), vs. IND (Dec. 1) Whom they're thankful for: Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas Cleveland has kept only one of its first-round picks since drafting Evan Mobley in 2021 (that was Jaylon Tyson), but this pair of second-round guards is giving the Cavaliers a much-needed infusion of young talent regardless. Proctor, drafted at No. 49 in 2025, is averaging 9.1 points and making 44% of his 3s. Thomas, drafted with the No. 34 pick in 2026, is averaging 12.7 points and shooting 41% from distance. -- Zach Kram Next games: @ HOU (Nov. 25), vs. DAL (Nov. 27), @ UTAH (Nov. 29), vs. LAC (Dec. 1) There are few things more reliable in the league than Booker putting the ball in the basket for the Suns. The franchise's all-time leading scorer is averaging 24.5 points this season -- his 10th straight season averaging 24 points or more -- and helped his team to eight wins in their past 10 games after starting the season 1-5. The fact that Booker has become a five-time All-Star with the same franchise while playing for enough head coaches to fill a cornucopia (eight different coaches in 12 years), is something Suns fans should not take for granted. -- McMenamin Next games: vs. SAC (Nov. 25), @ POR (Nov. 27), vs. LAC (Nov. 29), vs. UTAH (Dec. 1) Days before training camp, Curry opted to remove any drama about the late stages of his career, signing a two-year extension to deliver the front office an extra $10 million this summer in theoretical cap space and commit to the franchise through his 20th season. "I assumed it would probably be one of, if not the last, contract I signed," Curry told ESPN. "I'm not afraid to say it. But maybe I'll surprise myself and want to keep going." If Curry calls it a career after the 2028-29 season, it will close out two of the greatest individual one-franchise decades in league history. When on the court, he isn't fading quietly. Before his recent oblique injury, Curry was averaging 27.8 points in 26.3 minutes. -- Slater After an injury-filled 2025-26 season, Wagner is putting up All-NBA numbers with the Magic this season. The Magic are 18 points per 100 possessions better when Wagner is on the court this season. -- Marks After their first two seasons of finishing among the worst teams in the league, the Wizards still didn't have a franchise-altering star to show for all those defeats. In the 2024 draft, they landed the No. 2 pick and drafted Alex Sarr; in the 2025 draft, they fell all the way to No. 6 and landed Tre Johnson. But in a star-driven league like the NBA, one player can make all the difference. The Wizards hope they landed just that player when they won the 2026 lottery and selected Dybantsa at No. 1. -- Kram Next games: vs. BKN (Nov. 27), vs. DEN (Nov. 29), @ HOU (Dec. 1) Though Leonard has played in only two games this season as he manages left knee soreness, his presence in Toronto, paired with All-Star Scottie Barnes, makes this team at full strength a contender in the East. He has started 17 of the Pacers' 18 games, more than any other member of the starting lineup, and is averaging 22.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists on 51% shooting. Tyrese Haliburton posted a video to Instagram recently saying he hopes to return from his hamstring injury by the end of November, and he'll be thankful to have Siakam remaining steady by his side when he does. -- Jamal Collier Next games: @ CHA (Nov. 25), vs. IND (Nov. 28), vs. NYK (Dec. 1) After years of middling, miserable seasons, Chicago finally got a payoff last summer by jumping into the top four and landing one of the talented prospects at the top of the draft. Wilson is still a very raw prospect in several respects, but he has arrived in Chicago with confidence, explosiveness and highlight-worthy athleticism, and has given the Bulls their best hope since perhaps the early days of Derrick Rose. Even as Wilson recovers from a broken hand, the Bulls can be thankful for a new face of the franchise. -- Collier Next games: @ MEM (Nov. 25), vs. NO (Nov. 27), @ GS (Nov. 29), @ PHX (Dec. 1) Even in a rebuilding season, Garland has brought stability to the Clippers, averaging the eighth-most points per game (21.3) out of anybody in the top 15 in assists per game (6.6) this season. And at 26, the two-time All-Star is young enough to continue to grow with the team as it hopes to crawl back toward contention. Perhaps the biggest reason Clippers fans should be thankful for Garland's presence is it means 37-year-old James Harden is no longer on the roster. Though Harden is a sure-fire Hall of Famer, and recently turned back the clock with 51 points against the Indiana Pacers, the three-year, $97 million extension he signed with the Cleveland Cavaliers after LA traded him for Garland and a second-round pick is something the Clips would not want on their books going forward. -- McMenamin Next games: vs. CHI (Nov. 25), vs. BKN (Nov. 28), vs. WAS (Nov. 30) Diabate might be the hardest worker in the NBA, as the undersized center is willing himself to a league-leading 5.4 offensive rebounds per game. He originally arrived in Charlotte on a two-way contract in 2024, but he has since transformed into a valuable role player who should enjoy a lengthy career. -- Kram Next games: @ LAC (Nov. 27), @ POR (Nov. 29), @ SAC (Nov. 30) The Pelicans are off to a messy start: They've already suffered seven losses by double digits, and starting guard Dejounte Murray publicly requested a trade after playing only nine games. title: GS Group elevates fourth-generation founding family member to president as stability anchors reshuffle strategy - Korea JoongAng Daily
content: The conglomerate promoted GS Retail CEO Hur Suh-hong to president while retaining major affiliate chiefs and expanding its next generation of executives. GS Group promoted Hur Suh-hong, a fourth-generation member of its founding family and CEO of GS Retail, to president on Wednesday, while keeping the chief executives of its major affiliates in place. The 2027 reshuffle covers 40 executives: two promotions to president, four new CEOs, six promotions to senior executive vice president, four to senior vice president and 24 newly appointed vice presidents. Unlike last year, when GS replaced the CEOs of nine affiliates, this year's reshuffle prioritized management stability and business continuity. Hur Suh-hong is the eldest son of Samyang International Chairman Hur Kwang-soo, a cousin of GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo. Huh and Hur are different spellings of the same Korean surname. Hur Suh-hong worked at GS Energy and GS Holdings before becoming CEO of GS Retail. As head of the future business team at GS Holdings, he led the group's acquisition of botulinum toxin maker Hugel, which helped diversify its businesses. Since taking the helm, Hur Suh-hong has focused on strengthening GS Retail's core businesses and on transforming its operations through AI. GS Retail posted record quarterly consolidated revenue and operating profit in the third quarter this year, helped by record convenience store sales and sharply higher operating profit at its supermarket and home shopping businesses. The recovery in its core businesses and improvements to its business structure are seen as the reasons behind his promotion. Lee Tae-hyoung, the chief financial officer of GS Holdings and head of its portfolio management team, was also promoted to president. Born in 1970, he started out as an engineer at the Yeosu refinery of Honam Oil Refinery, now GS Caltex. He later served as head of corporate planning at GS Energy and CEO of Incheon Total Energy Company, a GS Energy subsidiary. Lee Tae-hyoung was credited with keeping the group's finances sound while supporting its search for new businesses such as AI data centers. He will now coordinate investment priorities and funding plans to back Chairman Huh Tae-soo's growth strategy. Other fourth-generation family members also took on bigger roles. Huh Joo-hong, a GS Caltex executive, and Huh Chi-hong, head of GS Retail's strategy division, were both promoted to senior executive vice president. Huh Joo-hong is the son of Huh Myung-soo, a standing adviser at GS Engineering & Construction (GS E&C), and Huh Chi-hong is the son of GS Caltex adviser Huh Jin-soo. Huh Joo-hong will head GS Caltex's chemicals and lubricants division, which oversees its petrochemical and lubricant businesses. Huh Chi-hong will coordinate GS Retail's companywide strategy and look for growth through overseas business and investment. GS also promoted executives who delivered results in the field and in management. Kim Ki-hwan of GS Energy has led its renewable energy and new business strategy, and Kim Young-ju of GS Caltex pushed for more efficient operations and digital transformation at its production sites. Kang Yoon-seok of GS Retail helped improve the company's earnings structure, and Sung Nag-hyun of GS E&C has three decades of procurement experience. All four were promoted to senior executive vice president. GS kept the CEOs of its major affiliates but nominated new chief executives for four energy and power generation subsidiaries. Kim Jin-hak was tapped for Incheon Total Energy Company, Lee Jong-jin for GS Gumi Combined Heat and Power Plant, Heo Chang-ik for GS Donghae Electric Power and Yeo Seung-sub for GS Banwol Combined Heat and Power Plant. The appointments are seen as a response to changes in the electricity market and an effort to keep the subsidiaries' power plants running reliably. The group also stepped up efforts to develop its next generation of leaders. GS named 24 new vice presidents, a 33.3 percent increase from 18 in each of the previous two reshuffles. Eight are in their 40s. GS E&C named 10 new executives, double the number in its previous reshuffle. The appointments span its core housing and urban redevelopment businesses as well as future growth areas such as property development and data centers. GS EPS put a new vice president in their 40s in charge of the future business division at its power policy headquarters. "With uncertainty high at home and abroad, we chose stability so that our major affiliates can carry on with the business innovation they have been pursuing," a GS official said. "We will continue to support each affiliate in strengthening the profitability and competitiveness of its core business and in finding new growth engines through cooperation among affiliates, so that they can deliver tangible results." Bloomberg reported that two Chinese companies participating in the Yangtze River Delta Project, a large-scale data center project, had installed server systems powered by Nvidia's Blackwell chips despite U.S. export restrictions While the fashion industry generally agrees that the Nvidia CEO's switch from his signature leather jacket to an understated cotton one appears to be an attempt to project humility and remorse, they have also noted the irony behind it costing $3,300. E9pay, a cross-border remittance service provider that had been preparing an initial public offering, or IPO, for a Kosdaq listing, reportedly lost about 2.5 billion won ($1.9 million) in a series of cyberattacks. Foreign shareholders accounted for 51 percent of Samsung Electronics' 30 trillion won ($22.5 billion) third quarter dividend payout, receiving a combined 15.3 trillion won, as the chipmaker ramped up shareholder returns.

title: BMW GS Rallye 2026 – Rain, Gravel and a Little GS That Could - Bike Rider Magazine
content: Nearly 160 riders, a weather forecast from hell and a route through the central North Island. Paul Lance heads to the BMW GS Rallye in Taupō aboard the new F 450 GS, discovering that you don’t need a massive adventure bike to have a massive amount of fun. There’s something rather satisfying about preparing for a big adventure ride. Getting the gear sorted, loading the GPS, checking the motorcycle and looking forward to a day exploring roads and tracks you’ve probably never ridden before. It’s even better when someone else has done all the hard work of finding the route. Unfortunately, there’s one thing the organisers of the BMW GS Rallye couldn’t control. And as I drove down to Taupō for the 2026 event, the forecast was becoming increasingly unpleasant. Heavy rain, thunderstorms and the sort of conditions that make you question whether spending an entire day on a motorcycle is really the best idea. By Saturday morning, those forecasts were proving depressingly accurate. The rain was absolutely hammering down, with nearly 160 riders preparing to head off into the countryside on everything from enormous BMW GS adventure tourers to smaller machines more suited to getting themselves into trouble. My motorcycle for the weekend was the new BMW F 450 GS Trophy, equipped with the clever Easy Ride Clutch system. I’d ridden the little BMW previously during our initial test, but this would be something different. A full day of road riding, gravel, forest tracks, mud, rain and whatever else the central North Island could throw at us. It was the sort of test that would reveal a lot more about the F 450 GS than another pleasant afternoon on dry gravel roads. And as it turned out, the little BMW was one of the stars of the weekend. This year’s GS Rallye was based at Wairakei Resort, just outside Taupō, with BMW Motorrad New Zealand taking a more direct role in organising the event. It was a slightly different approach from previous years. Rather than simply turning up for the ride and making your own accommodation arrangements, participants could book a package incorporating their accommodation, evening meals and breakfasts. That made the whole weekend feel more like a proper motorcycle rally, with everyone gathering in the same place rather than disappearing to accommodation scattered around the district. It also meant plenty of opportunities to catch up with familiar faces, meet new riders and discuss the various advantages of spending far too much money on adventure motorcycles. Moto Track and Trail helped plan and manage the riding, with routes supplied beforehand as GPX files. These could be loaded into a GPS unit or compatible navigation app, allowing riders to follow the route at their own pace. There were three main choices: a sealed-road ride, a gravel-focused route and a gravel route incorporating optional technical breakouts. The main adventure route would head north towards Ōtorohanga for lunch and fuel before making its way back towards Taupō. Having attended the previous GS Rallye, where we’d tackled plenty of gravel and some fairly challenging terrain, I’d initially been looking forward to the optional breakouts. But with the weather forecast deteriorating by the hour, I was beginning to reconsider that enthusiasm. Perhaps discretion really was the better part of valour. Then again, that would depend on how much fun everyone else appeared to be having. Saturday morning arrived with the sort of rain that makes you wonder whether you should be building an ark rather than preparing a motorcycle. Friends and family were sending me videos showing terrible conditions elsewhere in the country, and all that weather appeared to be heading directly towards Taupō. I decided there was no point taking chances with my riding gear. Over my usual Leatt adventure equipment went a set of Scott waterproofs, effectively adding another layer between me and the elements. I also treated the inside of my visor to help prevent fogging and applied a water-repellent product to the outside. The idea was simple: stay as dry as possible, keep the visor clear and hopefully avoid spending the day wondering whether my socks were turning into small aquariums. Once I reached the more technical tracks and needed to open my visor to see where I was going, rain found its way onto the inside. At that point, all the preparation in the world becomes rather academic. You can polish the outside of your visor as much as you like, but when there’s water running down the inside, visibility becomes considerably more interesting. Meanwhile, the rain showed absolutely no sign of giving up. I let the main group of motorcycles head off first so I could film the departure. Then I climbed aboard the F 450 GS and set off in pursuit, making sure I stayed ahead of the sweep rider. The first thing that struck me was how easy the BMW was to ride. It’s a compact motorcycle, with a narrow waist, accessible riding position and very little of the bulk you associate with the larger GS models. On my test bike, I could put both feet firmly on the ground. That’s reassuring when you’re setting off into unknown terrain, particularly with the weather doing its best to make everything slippery. I’d fitted a Quad Lock phone mount to the handlebars, downloaded BMW’s Motorrad Connected app to my iPhone and paired the phone with the bike’s TFT dashboard via Bluetooth. That let me follow the route using navigation information on the BMW’s display, which was particularly useful when exploring unfamiliar roads. Unfortunately, as I would discover later, having a route displayed on a screen doesn’t necessarily prevent you from getting lost. The opening part of the route included rather more sealed road than I’d expected. Compared with the previous year’s event, which had featured extensive gravel riding and some quite challenging sections, this route was clearly designed to be more accessible. And looking around at the enormous variety of motorcycles taking part, I could understand why. There were plenty of large-capacity GS models, many carrying enough accessories to fund a reasonable family holiday. Their owners weren’t necessarily looking to throw them down a slippery hillside or spend half the day digging them out of a bog. Not everyone who owns an adventure motorcycle wants to compete in the International Six Days Enduro. Eventually I arrived at one of the optional technical sections. A marshal was stationed at the entrance, and I asked what the track was like. Nothing too difficult, apparently. Just a straightforward bit of riding through the bush. The good news was that the volcanic soil around Taupō drains remarkably well. Despite the torrential rain, we weren’t riding through endless deep mud, although the tracks were certainly slippery enough to demand concentration. The route wound through tight forest trails, climbing and descending between trees before reaching a short hill with a corner partway up. A couple of larger motorcycles became stuck, and before long there was a queue of bikes waiting to get through. Eventually we reached another group of riders standing beside a locked gate. Apparently, in dry conditions it would have been fairly straightforward. In the rain, however, even some of the more experienced riders were struggling to get up it. The organisers had sensibly decided to divert everyone through the gate instead. “When the marshal arrived to unlock it, he dropped the key into the long grass. And couldn’t find it.” When the marshal arrived to unlock it, he dropped the key into the long grass. Unfortunately, a small group of us ended up following a track that seemed to become progressively less used, until we were negotiating fallen branches, logs, long grass and narrow trails that didn’t look as though they’d seen a motorcycle in years. At some point we collectively decided that perhaps we weren’t heading in quite the right direction. Turning around eventually brought us back to other riders, and after a little more exploring we finally found our way out. The whole episode was a reminder that adventure riding doesn’t always go to plan. But it also demonstrated just how manageable the little BMW was in difficult conditions. I’d previously experienced BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch during our original F 450 GS test, but a day like this was an excellent opportunity to find out whether the system offered any real benefit. The system uses a centrifugal clutch that engages automatically as engine speed rises, meaning you can pull away without operating the clutch lever. Combined with BMW’s Shift Assistant Pro, you can also change up and down through the six-speed gearbox without touching the clutch. But throughout most of the Rallye, I simply didn’t bother. “And after spending most of the day without touching the clutch lever, I was thoroughly convinced of its benefits.” Initially, I’d wondered whether needing to bring the engine above approximately 2500rpm to engage the clutch might make the rear wheel more likely to spin in slippery conditions. The engagement was smooth and progressive, with plenty of traction available even on wet gravel and forest tracks. It was particularly useful when negotiating technical sections, where the last thing you want is to be constantly juggling the clutch while trying to maintain balance and find traction. Even when crossing small logs or obstacles, I found myself simply using the throttle rather than deliberately slipping the clutch. The system isn’t a substitute for riding technique, and there will be situations where experienced off-road riders prefer manual clutch control. But for the kind of adventure riding we were doing, it made life considerably easier. And after spending most of the day without touching the clutch lever, I was thoroughly convinced of its benefits. The F 450 GS is powered by a newly developed 420cc parallel-twin producing a claimed 35kW (48hp) and 43Nm. With a ready-to-ride weight of 178kg in standard specification, it sits at the lighter end of BMW’s adventure range. The engine uses a 135-degree crankpin arrangement, giving it a distinctive character, while the compact chassis incorporates a tubular steel frame, 19-inch front and 17-inch rear wheels, and 180mm of suspension travel at both ends. There’s a substantial electronics package, too, including riding modes, traction control and ABS Pro. My test bike was the GS Trophy version, wearing its Racing blue metallic paintwork with red and white details. It also came equipped with features particularly relevant to a day like this, including handguards, enduro footrests, an aluminium bashplate and a taller tinted screen. For the Rallye, I selected Enduro mode and disabled the rear ABS. That was pretty much where I left the settings for the entire day. The system reduced traction-control intervention and gave me enough freedom to move the rear wheel around on gravel without constantly fighting the electronics. In Enduro mode, the initial response felt a little softer than I’d ideally like. Personally, I prefer a slightly more immediate throttle when riding enthusiastically on gravel, particularly when using the rear wheel to help steer the motorcycle. In fact, once I started enjoying the flowing gravel sections, I was surprised by just how easily I could slide the little BMW through corners. You don’t necessarily need enormous horsepower to have fun on gravel. Sometimes having a lighter motorcycle with accessible performance is much more entertaining. The F 450 GS made that point repeatedly throughout the day. After escaping the forest tracks, the route continued north towards Ōtorohanga. There were more sealed roads, more gravel and, at one point, a navigation system that seemed determined to send me somewhere entirely different. I found myself following a sealed road with the GPS suggesting I had another 43km to travel before turning. Eventually I stopped, studied the route and realised I’d wandered away from the intended track. A little retracing soon had me back where I belonged. “You don’t necessarily need enormous horsepower to have fun on gravel.” Long, flowing, undulating stretches where you could see well ahead, settle into a rhythm and simply enjoy the way the motorcycle moved beneath you. Despite its modest power output, there was enough performance to accelerate strongly out of corners and use the rear wheel to help steer. The narrow chassis made it easy to move the bike around beneath me, and I actually spent much of the gravel riding sitting down. Rather than fighting the motorcycle or constantly shifting my weight, I could simply guide it into corners, let the rear move a little and drive out the other side. The BMW has a single 310mm front disc with a four-piston Brembo caliper, and there’s plenty of stopping power available. With the GPS warning of a junction a couple of hundred metres ahead, I could leave the braking reasonably late and trust the system to slow the motorcycle effectively. That combination of light weight, accurate handling and strong brakes made the F 450 GS exceptionally confidence-inspiring. Eventually we reached Ōtorohanga, where the organisers had arranged for a local café to accommodate the incoming riders. There were motorcycles everywhere, with riders grabbing coffee, sandwiches, fuel and a chance to warm up. I headed for the petrol station, filled the BMW and sorted out some supplies before continuing. One of my smarter decisions had been packing a second pair of waterproof gloves. By lunchtime, the first pair was thoroughly soaked. It’s remarkable how much better you feel when your hands are warm and dry. Unfortunately, that doesn’t necessarily apply to the rest of your body. Despite the waterproof gear, water was gradually finding its way into places it really had no business being. And as it turned out, the afternoon would provide some of the best sections of the entire Rallye. After lunch, the route opened up into some truly superb gravel riding. There were long, sweeping roads with smooth surfaces, flowing bends and undulations that made the ride feel almost effortless. Fourth, fifth and occasionally sixth gear, with the BMW moving gently beneath me as I flowed from one corner to the next. There was enough traction to get on the throttle early, enough power to make things entertaining and not so much weight that the motorcycle felt like hard work. Eventually we entered another forest section, where the tracks became more overgrown and the riding a little more technical. There were large holes filled with water, fallen branches and a few places where choosing the right line became rather important. This was also where the BMW’s suspension limitations became more apparent. The F 450 GS has 180mm of suspension travel, but it’s an adventure motorcycle rather than a dedicated enduro bike. The suspension is deliberately controlled rather than extremely soft and plush, which helps make it such a good road motorcycle. But hit a particularly deep hole or sharp obstacle and you’re reminded that there’s only so much suspension travel available. I found myself standing on the footpegs more often through these sections, using my legs to absorb the bigger impacts. And while there wasn’t enough power to effortlessly lift the front wheel over obstacles with a twist of the throttle, a little body movement and careful application of power usually did the job. There was no need to worry about stalling or constantly covering the clutch lever. Eventually the gravel gave way to more sealed roads, and we began making our way back towards Taupō. A few other riders caught up, and we enjoyed a spirited run through some excellent winding roads. The little BMW was just as entertaining on the tarmac as it had been on gravel. There were only a handful of motorcycles ahead of us, although some riders had chosen the sealed-road route or may have returned earlier. Over the following hour, more bikes began arriving. There were plenty of tired faces, dirty motorcycles and riders who looked as though they’d enjoyed themselves enormously. Fortunately, the weather had improved during the afternoon, allowing us to dry out a little before returning. Peeling off the waterproof layers revealed the usual problems. My boots had leaked, which meant my socks were wet. The moisture had then worked its way up into the bottom of my trousers. Meanwhile, water running down my neck tube had found its way into my shirt. The waterproof outer layers had done a pretty good job, but water is remarkably inventive when it comes to finding a way inside your clothing. I was also beginning to appreciate the BMW’s heated grips, which I’d discovered partway through the day. A particularly welcome feature when your gloves have spent several hours pretending to be dishcloths. By the time we returned, I’d covered close to 450km across a mixture of sealed roads, gravel and forest tracks. That’s a substantial day on any adventure motorcycle, particularly in conditions like those we’d encountered. It has enough performance to make the bike entertaining without constantly demanding attention, and the smooth power delivery makes it easy to find traction on slippery surfaces. The chassis is wonderfully manageable, with a riding position that gives you confidence and a narrow shape that makes it easy to move around. The front brake is particularly impressive, while the suspension strikes a useful compromise between road comfort and off-road ability. At 182cm tall, I found the riding position a little cramped after such a long day, and my backside was beginning to complain by the time we reached Wairakei. But then we’d spent the best part of a day riding nearly 450km, much of it in fairly demanding conditions. I’d probably have been uncomfortable on just about anything by that stage. The suspension also reminds you that this isn’t a hardcore enduro motorcycle when the terrain gets particularly rough. The F 450 GS is an accessible, versatile adventure bike that’s capable of taking riders well beyond ordinary sealed roads. And with the Easy Ride Clutch, it’s one of the most approachable motorcycles of its kind. Looking back on the weekend, I think BMW deserves considerable credit for the event. The weather could easily have turned it into a miserable experience, yet the organisers managed to keep everything running and provide a memorable day for a large group of riders. The route was certainly more road-focused than I’d expected. Personally, I’d have preferred a little more gravel, particularly given how good the afternoon sections were. But that needs to be considered in the context of who was attending. There were riders of varying abilities, on motorcycles ranging from smaller adventure machines to very large, expensive GS models. “You really don’t need a massive adventure motorcycle to have a massive adventure.” I spoke to a couple of riders who’d attended the previous event and had found the technical terrain so demanding that they’d only managed to reach the lunch stop before deciding to return. That tells you something about the challenges of organising an event like this. Make it too difficult, and some riders won’t enjoy themselves. Make it too easy, and the more experienced riders may feel they’ve missed out on an adventure. The optional breakouts were a sensible solution, allowing riders to choose additional challenges without forcing everyone into difficult terrain. Had the weather been better, I’m sure those sections would have been particularly enjoyable. The other thing I liked was seeing motorcycles from other manufacturers taking part. Alongside the BMWs were KTMs, Yamaha Ténérés and other adventure bikes. At the end of the day, the point isn’t simply to promote one brand. It’s to get riders out enjoying their motorcycles, exploring new places and meeting people who share the same enthusiasm. And judging by the tired but happy faces returning to Wairakei, BMW achieved exactly that. I went into the BMW GS Rallye expecting a good day’s riding and an opportunity to spend more time with the new F 450 GS. There was torrential rain, slippery forest tracks, a missing gate key, some navigational confusion and some of the best flowing gravel roads I’ve ridden in a while. And through it all, the little BMW was outstanding. I’d already been impressed by the F 450 GS during our original test, but a long day in genuinely challenging conditions confirmed just how capable it is. The Easy Ride Clutch was particularly impressive, removing one more thing to worry about when riding technical terrain and making the motorcycle exceptionally easy to manage. There were times when I wished for slightly sharper throttle response in Enduro mode and a little more suspension compliance over bigger obstacles. But those are relatively minor criticisms of a motorcycle that managed everything I asked of it. And the whole experience reinforced something I’ve been thinking for a while. You really don’t need a massive adventure motorcycle to have a massive adventure. Sometimes a smaller, lighter bike is exactly what you want.
